name: Lip stencil / bone structure hack: orthotropics for lip support

card.summary: The claim that mewing reshapes bone to support the lips; reference sources call mewing unproven and do not cover lips.
card.note: Experts cited say no credible evidence supports mewing changing facial structure.

quick.overview:
This is the idea that mewing, a tongue and jaw posture practice from orthotropics, can change the lip profile by altering the bone beneath the lips.

Reference sources describe mewing as unproven and say orthodontic bodies see no evidence it reshapes the jaw.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners press the tongue against the palate and keep a sealed-lip, nasal-breathing posture, believing sustained posture shifts jaw growth and facial support.
quick.risks: Potential risks cited include jaw joint problems, bite changes and delayed orthodontic care in children.

lead: This entry covers the claim, circulated in mewing and orthotropics circles, that jaw and facial posture training can change the profile of the lips by altering the bone structure that supports them. People pursue it hoping for fuller-looking, better-supported lips and a more balanced profile without cosmetic procedures. Mewing is a form of oral posture training associated with orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, built on resting the tongue against the roof of the mouth.[1]

Proponents reason that if the upper jaw and teeth sit further forward, the lips gain support and a different profile. Orthodontic research does show that lips follow tooth movement: in a 2020 University of Iowa study of 60 adults treated with braces, horizontal upper lip movement matched upper incisor crown movement at roughly a one-to-one ratio.[3] Those findings concern orthodontic tooth movement, not posture training.

Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven form of oral posture training, states that no credible scientific research has proven the efficacy of orthotropics, and reports that the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it improves the jaw. It does not address lips or soft tissue.[1][2]

chain: Claimed forward or wider jaw and palate
Claimed fuller lip support and profile
angle.text: Practitioners hope that changing the bone and teeth behind the lips will push the lips forward for a fuller profile. Research shows lips respond to tooth position, but not that posture training moves bone.

infobox: Upper lip moved about 1:1 with upper incisor in one braces study [3]

paras: Orthotropics holds that oral posture guides jaw and facial growth, in contrast to conventional orthodontics, which focuses on aligning teeth.[2] The lip-related claim extends this: if the jaws move forward or the upper jaw widens, the lips are said to gain support and a different profile. The reference articles on mewing do not describe lip outcomes.[1][2]

Mewing is named after British orthodontist John Mew. His son Mike Mew is also associated with it; Wikipedia reports Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and, in 2024, struck from the UK dental register after a misconduct hearing involving child patients. Mewing went viral on social media from 2019, especially within looksmaxxing subcultures.[1]

sections.h: Teeth, bone and lip position in orthodontics
paras: In conventional orthodontics, lip position changes with incisor movement. The 2020 Iowa cephalometric thesis of 30 extraction and 30 non-extraction adult cases found upper lip movement tracked the upper incisor crown at roughly 1:1, and that upper incisor angulation increased about 6.8 degrees in the non-extraction group and decreased about 4.3 degrees in the extraction group.[3] Other orthodontic work on lip response varies between individuals, according to the authors of these studies, and that research concerns braces rather than posture training.

The American Association of Orthodontists and the Cleveland Clinic are reported to state that there is no credible scientific evidence that mewing reshapes the face or jawline.[2] Wikipedia says most orthodontists do not consider mewing a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery.[1] Potential risks cited for the practice include temporomandibular joint disorders, bite problems and delayed orthodontic care in children.[2]

No studies found on orthotropics or mewing changing lip profile. Related work exists on orofacial myofunctional therapy: 2025 pilot studies reported effects on hyoid position and jaw pain, but they did not directly test mewing or lip outcomes.[2] Separate orthodontic research on tooth movement and lip position is described above.[3]

timeline.event: Mewing goes viral on social media, especially in looksmaxxing communities.[1]
Mike Mew is struck from the UK dental register.[1]

lore.intro: Mewing communities discuss lip support as one possible by-product of posture training, alongside jawline and midface claims.

claims.claim: Mewing can change lip profile by moving the underlying bone structure.
claims.believers: Proponents say better tongue and oral posture advances the maxilla and jaw, giving the lips more support and a fuller profile.
claims.experts: The AAO and Cleveland Clinic are reported to state there is no credible evidence that mewing reshapes the face.[2] No published study tests lip profile change from mewing; orthodontic studies show lips follow incisor movement with braces.[3]
